title: Fiduccia–Mattheyses Refinement
hook: The node with the biggest gain is not allowed to move. What does the algorithm do?
cardText: Move one node at a time, keeping both sides inside the balance window. Only legal moves count; exploring, locking and the best prefix work as in KL.
description: Single-node moves: choose the largest gain among balance-legal nodes, explore negative gains, roll back to the best prefix at the end of a pass; includes the disproved original counterexample, a replacement verified by exhaustive search, and multi-pin nets.
prerequisitesText: [Module 07](../m07-kernighan-lin/index.html): gains, locks, trials and the best prefix.
nextText: Module 09 changes the goal from the cut to delay, and allows nodes to be copied.
review: Module 07’s four ideas carry over unchanged: **gain, lock, trial and best prefix** (the empty prefix included). Only one thing differs: KL swaps a pair at a time, FM **moves one node** at a time, so a balance window has to limit the side sizes.

objectives.text: State how FM differs from KL: single moves plus a balance window |n₀ − n₁| ≤ maxDiff, instead of one for one.
Choose the largest gain among the balance-legal unlocked nodes only: on the seed, A and E gain +6 but are not legal, so D (+3) is chosen.
Split a gain into FS and TE: D has FS = DE (5) and TE = CD (2), gain 3; after D moves, A becomes a legal +6.
Walk through one pass (cut 12, 9, 3, 5, 11, 12), choose the best prefix k* = 2, and tell the trial state from the accepted one.
Audit the attachment’s hillclimb claim, and use an exhaustively verified example to show what negative gains are for.
Tell “drawing buckets” from “a linear-time implementation”, and 2-pin graphs from real multi-pin nets; implement gain and the legal candidates in Python.

problem.input: A weighted 2-pin graph (or a multi-pin netlist), an initial bisection, and the balance parameter maxDiff.
problem.output: For each pass: the trial moves (node, gain, FS/TE, cut after the move), the cumulative gains and the best prefix; then the accepted bisection, the final cut and the stop reason.
problem.objective: Lower the cut by single-node moves (with multi-pin nets: the total weight of the cut nets).
problem.constraints: After a move both sides are nonempty and |n₀ − n₁| ≤ maxDiff (counting nodes); each node moves at most once per pass.
problem.assumptions: Gains may be negative; take the largest gain among legal candidates, ties by node name; on a tie for the best prefix the shorter one wins; the empty prefix is allowed.
problem.stop: A pass whose best prefix is empty, or the pass limit.

filmNote: The popular-science film puts the five friends in two rooms of three beds, moving one at a time, the rooms differing by one at most: Ada and Eva would save the most but may not move, Dev may, and then Ada can; the losses are tried too, and it rolls back to the best prefix; with six other people two small losses buy a gain of 4; and the empty prefix ends it. The concise film covers FM versus KL and the balance window, legality before the largest gain, the FS/TE split, one pass of trial moves, the best prefix and the stop; the advanced film covers a negative-gain example verified exhaustively, an audit of the attachment’s hillclimb claim (used only as material on how to audit an example), multi-pin nets counted by pins, buckets and what “linear time” does and does not mean, and count versus area balance; the lab walkthrough, recorded from the real page, takes you through the lab and the in-browser code once. Every value comes from this page’s engine.
labNote: Each step lists every node’s gain, whether it is legal, the FS/TE breakdown, and the nodes grouped by gain into “buckets”. The buckets are rebuilt by a scan each step: a teaching implementation, not the paper’s linear-time bucket structure.
challengeTip: In question 3, “keep 0 steps” is a valid answer too; question 6 is the multi-pin extension.

mistakes.title: Picking the node with the largest gain outright
mistakes.wrong: On seed AE | BCD, move A first (gain +6).
mistakes.why: A is on the left, which has only 2 nodes; moving it leaves 1 there, and |1 − 4| = 3 > 1 breaks the balance.
mistakes.counter: The legal candidates are only B (+1), C (−4) and D (+3); choose D. Once D has moved across, A becomes a legal +6.
mistakes.fix: Filter for legality first, then take the largest gain among the legal candidates.

mistakes.title: Copying the attachment’s hillclimb claim
mistakes.wrong: The text: “initial cut 9, every legal move has gain ≤ 0; FM first takes −1, then gains +6, down to 4.”
mistakes.why: Computed from the attachment’s own data, the initial cut is 18; E’s move is legal with gain +10; pass 1’s best cut is 8, and the exhaustive balanced optimum is 8 too. The text does not match the data.
mistakes.counter: This course’s replacement: initial cut 6, every legal move has gain ≤ 0; FM takes −1, −1, then gains +4, keeps 3 steps, cut 4, and exhaustive search confirms that is the balanced optimum.
mistakes.fix: Verify an example with an independent computation (each legal move’s gain plus the exhaustive optimum) before it goes into teaching material.

mistakes.title: Taking “buckets drawn” for “linear time implemented”
mistakes.wrong: The page shows nodes grouped by gain into buckets, so the implementation is claimed to be O(P).
mistakes.why: The paper’s linear time comes from incrementally maintained bucket lists and a max-gain pointer; the attachment’s and this course’s teaching implementations scan every candidate at each step.
mistakes.counter: This course updates gains incrementally (recomputing only the nodes on affected nets), but selection is still a scan: it cannot be called O(P).
mistakes.fix: Keep “the complexity of the algorithm in theory” and “the complexity of this implementation” apart.

mistakes.title: Calling an ordinary-edge example a hypergraph
mistakes.wrong: The attachment’s third case has the id hypergraph, but its data are 2-pin edges only.
mistakes.why: A real multi-pin net decides FS/TE by counting its pins on each side; splitting the net into edges first gives different results.
mistakes.counter: Net {A,B,C,D} (weight 3) with A, B, C on the left and D on the right: counting pins, A’s gain is 0 (the net stays cut after A moves); split into a clique (3/(4−1) = 1 per pair) and counted by edges, A’s “gain” is 1 − 2 = −1.
mistakes.fix: When multi-pin nets matter, count pins (this course’s engine supports it, marked as an extension).

mistakes.title: Thinking count balance is area balance
mistakes.wrong: Believing maxDiff limits the area of each side.
mistakes.why: This chapter counts nodes; with cells of different areas the window has to be defined by area.
mistakes.counter: A cell of area 10 and a cell of area 1 count “the same” in a head-count window.
mistakes.fix: When area balance is needed, define legality by summed area instead (not implemented in this course, marked as an extension).

limits:
- The base track of this chapter is weighted 2-pin graphs; multi-pin nets are a marked extension (the engine already updates gains by counting pins). A balance window weighted by area is not implemented.
- The teaching implementation’s selection step is a scan, so it does not reach the 1982 paper’s O(P) per pass.
- FM is a heuristic: reaching the balanced optimum on G01 and on the replacement example is a property of those two graphs.
- The result depends on the initial bisection and the tie rule (this course: gain descending, then node name). The attachment’s tie rule (on equal gain prefer moving from the larger side, names in reverse) differs, so the move order in some cases differs.

pythonPackage.title: Implement gain and the legal candidates
pythonPackage.md:
**Tasks** (`starter.py`):

1. `gain(nets, side, v)`: return (gain, FS list, TE list), counting each net’s pins per side; this works for multi-pin nets too.
2. `legal_moves(side, locked, max_diff)`: the unlocked nodes that are still balanced after moving.

**Hint 1**: for each net that contains v, count its pins on v’s side (F) and on the other side (T): only v on F → +w; none on T → −w.

**Hint 2**: use `balance_ok({**side, v: 1 - side[v]}, max_diff)` to decide whether a move is legal. The checker audits the attachment’s hillclimb data, and checks gain = cut before − cut after on 150 random graphs (multi-pin nets included).

kept: The single-page Chinese workshop: stepping, undo, the best prefix, a full pass, the gain breakdown, the bucket display and a projector mode (this chapter’s lab keeps the “white-box” idea).
The walk-through of the original seed: D (+3), A (+6), cut 12 → 9 → 3, best k* = 2, no improvement in the next pass (reproduced by this course).
The “compare KL with FM” idea from the 10 tasks and 5 self-test questions, distilled into active challenges.
The hillclimb case’s data, kept as a regression test to show how to audit an example.
